notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Gum trees (eucalyptus) are by far the most common tree, with light bark and puffy clusters of leaves; their look varies by region.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: White bollard with a red reflector on the front and a grey one on the back; the red stops mid-bollard, unlike the neighbour's end-to-end wrap.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Traffic drives on the left.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Road lines are almost always white; yellow ones appear only in rare alpine areas. Yellow edge lines would suggest South Africa, a yellow centre line New Zealand.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Edge lines sometimes have small white rumble stripes across them, though rarely in the Northern Territory.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Give-way signs have a white border and black text; the neighbour's use red text.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are white on black or black on yellow, with no thin border or speed limit on the yellow ones.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Green intersection signs with white arrows list nearby towns, sometimes with distances in kilometres. Highways have alphanumeric names like A2 or C222.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Speed limit signs show black text in a red circle on a large white rectangle.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 3 shows a long antenna.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Phone numbers have 8 digits plus a 2-digit area code that is not always written.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Each state has its own bus stop design; Tasmanian ones mostly say 'metro' and Darwin's are usually concrete shelters.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: The iconic Stobie pole, steel and concrete with a trident or rotated-E top, belongs to the southern state, with a few elsewhere, mainly Tasmania.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Rusty metal poles with several holes are unique to the Northern Territory and appear around Wyndham in the far north of WA.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Queensland poles have tops with coils angled upwards at the sides, often with round blue stickers.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Victorian pole tops show three circular coils: one on each side and one on top.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Tasmanian pole tops often use a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees into an L shape; poles there wear olive-green possum guards.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: In WA a trident-like pole top has red insulators and a black crossbar; poles often have green bases and a red-and-white band.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Black-and-white striped bollards and bollards with a large brown base are mostly found in WA.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Yellow signposts, often flat rather than round, belong to WA.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland, and road signs with fluorescent borders are almost only seen there.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: New South Wales is the only state with red 'No Stopping' signs; a guardrail end with a black dash on yellow is almost exclusive to NSW and ACT.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Fire hydrants with red-painted tops and white hydrant poles with a blue circle are unique to Victoria.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A 130 km/h speed limit exists only in the Northern Territory.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Around Darwin: dark red soil, rich green grass and trees with black trunks; termite mounds are also seen in the Northern Territory.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical, with palms, dark green vegetation and widespread sugarcane.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: A cool temperate climate with green rolling hills and dense eucalyptus forests, comparable to Chile or New Zealand.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Inland NSW is flat with pale-green dry shrubs and soil that reddens the further inland you go.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The Nullarbor Highway is flat, grey and almost treeless, with very low vegetation.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Around Mount Gambier: white soil and extensive pine plantations.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Kangaroo Island has bushes, low stubby gum trees and orange soil like WA; only Generation 2 and 4 coverage exists there.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The Stuart Highway south of the Alice Springs area has bright orange dirt, short trees and a blue Generation 4 car.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: All-yellow road lines appear on roads near Mount Kosciuszko and in other alpine areas of Victoria and NSW.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Many rare Google cars with snorkels are in NSW and the ACT, with only two snorkel cars elsewhere, both in WA.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Two remote Indian Ocean island groups count as part of this country for streaks and have their own unique cars.
